address_cn: 四川省成都市青羊区少城路12号
hook: Chengdu's living room — where locals spend entire afternoons drinking tea from lidded bowls, getting their ears cleaned with tuning forks, and parents pin up dating profiles for their single adult children on clotheslines.
honest_description: People's Park is not a tourist attraction in the traditional sense — it's a window into how Chengdu locals actually live. The star is Heming Teahouse, a century-old outdoor tea garden where hundreds of bamboo chairs fill up every afternoon with people sipping gaiwan tea, playing mahjong, napping, gossiping, and having their ears cleaned by roaming specialists with tuning-fork instruments. The matchmaking corner (especially on weekends) is a fascinating cultural phenomenon where parents post detailed resumes of their unmarried children on paper sheets, hoping to find them a spouse. The park also contains genuine historical significance — the Railway Protection Movement monument commemorates Sichuan's role in the 1911 revolution. There are also a lake with paddle boats, bonsai and orchid gardens, morning tai chi groups, and dancing circles. It's free, central, and genuinely atmospheric. The downsides: it can be extremely crowded on weekends and holidays, the tea areas get noisy, and there's almost nothing in English. But this is exactly the kind of authentic local experience that guidebooks can't manufacture. Best for anyone who wants to feel the rhythm of Chengdu life rather than tick off sightseeing boxes.

foreigner_top_questions.question: Is this worth visiting as a tourist, or is it just a regular park?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: It's far more than a regular park — it's one of the most authentic cultural experiences in Chengdu. Sitting in the Heming Teahouse surrounded by locals playing mahjong, watching the ear-cleaning artists work, and browsing the matchmaking corner are experiences you simply cannot have anywhere else. Many foreign visitors rank this as a highlight of their Chengdu trip. Budget 2-3 hours to soak it in rather than rushing through.

foreigner_top_questions.question: How do I order tea at the teahouse?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: Just find an empty bamboo chair and sit down. A server will come to you. Point at what others are drinking or use your phone to translate. Popular choices: zhuyeqing (竹叶青, green tea, ~¥20-30), jasmine (茉莉花, ~¥15-20), or chrysanthemum (菊花, ~¥15). You'll get a traditional gaiwan (lidded bowl) and a thermos of hot water for unlimited refills. You can sit for hours without being pressured to leave or order more. Tea prices start around ¥16.

experience_format_note: Free-entry urban park open all day. No tickets or reservations needed. Multiple entrances from surrounding streets. The park is a casual, drop-in experience — there's no set route or must-follow path. The main draw is the teahouse culture and people-watching, not specific exhibits. Sichuan Opera face-changing performances are sometimes available at Heming Teahouse for ¥48. The matchmaking corner is most active on weekends, especially Saturday and Sunday afternoons. Morning is best for tai chi and dancing; afternoon for teahouse culture.
vibe: Gloriously unhurried — like discovering that an entire city has collectively agreed to slow down, drink tea, and not worry about anything for the next few hours.

time_needed.quick_visit: 1 hour (walk through, quick tea, glance at matchmaking corner)
time_needed.recommended: 2-3 hours (sit at Heming Teahouse for an hour, browse matchmaking corner, walk the gardens and lake)
time_needed.deep_dive: Half day (morning tai chi, long tea session, watch Sichuan Opera performance, explore all gardens and monuments)

best_time.best_time_of_day: Early morning (7-9 AM) for tai chi and dancing groups in a peaceful atmosphere. Afternoon (2-5 PM) for peak teahouse culture when all the bamboo chairs fill up. Weekend afternoons for the matchmaking corner at its most active.
best_time.worst_time: Chinese public holidays — the park becomes uncomfortably packed and loses its relaxed character. The autumn chrysanthemum festival (free but crowded) draws huge crowds. Rainy days dampen the outdoor tea experience.
best_time.seasonal_notes: Spring (March-May) is ideal — warm enough for outdoor tea, blooming magnolias and cherry trees. Autumn brings the famous chrysanthemum exhibition. Summer is hot and humid but the tree canopy provides shade. Winter is mild in Chengdu but the outdoor tea experience is less comfortable.
best_time.pro_tip: Come on a weekday afternoon for the best balance of authentic atmosphere and manageable crowds. The teahouse is at its most photogenic when afternoon light filters through the trees. Combine with a walk to Kuanzhai Alley (10 minutes on foot) afterward.

getting_in.opening_hours: Open daily. Summer: 06:00–22:30. Winter: 06:30–22:00. Teahouses typically open until 19:00. Amusement rides: 09:00–18:00.

getting_in.booking_method: No booking needed for any activity. Just arrive and participate.
getting_in.passport_accepted: Not applicable — free entry, no ID needed.
getting_in.what_to_bring: Cash or mobile payment for tea and services. Camera for the matchmaking corner and teahouse scenes. Comfortable shoes for walking the park.
getting_in.queue_situation: No queues for park entry. The teahouse can be standing-room-only on weekend afternoons — arrive early to secure a bamboo chair. The matchmaking corner is free-flowing, no queue.
getting_in.language_barrier_rating: significant-barrier — Almost nothing is in English. Tea menus are Chinese-only. The matchmaking profiles are all in Chinese. However, the experience is highly visual and atmospheric — you don't need to read Chinese to enjoy sitting in the teahouse, watching the ear-cleaning artists, or soaking in the atmosphere. If you want to understand what the matchmaking profiles say or need help ordering tea, our concierge can translate in real time via chat — just send us a photo.

highlights.name: Heming Teahouse (鹤鸣茶社)
highlights.description: Operating since 1923, this is one of Chengdu's most iconic teahouses — hundreds of bamboo chairs spread under ancient trees by a lake, filled with locals drinking gaiwan tea, playing mahjong, reading, napping, and chatting. The long-spout teapot pouring performance is a classic Chengdu spectacle. Ear-cleaning artists roam the area offering the unique Chengdu specialty.
highlights.foreigner_note: This is the definitive Chengdu local experience. You don't need to speak Chinese — just sit down, order tea by pointing, and observe. The ear-cleaning service (using tuning forks and fine tools) looks alarming but is actually relaxing and has been a Chengdu tradition for centuries.
highlights.tip: Arrive by 1-2 PM on a weekday to grab a good chair. Order the cheapest tea — the experience is the same regardless of price. Sit near the lake for the best atmosphere. Plan to stay at least an hour.

highlights.name: Matchmaking Corner (相亲角)
highlights.description: Near the south entrance, parents pin up paper profiles of their unmarried adult children — complete with age, height, weight, education, job, salary, and property ownership status. Pink sheets for women, blue for men. Parents browse, compare, and negotiate potential matches. It's essentially analog Tinder, run by parents.
highlights.foreigner_note: This is a genuinely fascinating cultural phenomenon. In China, unmarried adults (especially over 27) face enormous family pressure. Some parents visit every weekend for months or years. Foreign visitors have been known to have their own profiles posted by enthusiastic local parents.
highlights.tip: Visit on a Saturday or Sunday afternoon (2-5 PM) for the most active matchmaking scene. It's perfectly acceptable to browse and photograph — just be respectful and don't mock anyone.

highlights.name: Morning Activities (Tai Chi, Dancing, Calligraphy)
highlights.description: Every morning, the park fills with groups doing tai chi, sword dancing, fan dancing, ballroom dancing, water calligraphy on the pavement, and various exercises. Each group has its own spot and routine. Visitors are often welcomed to join.
highlights.foreigner_note: The morning tai chi groups are happy to have you join — just follow along. The water calligraphers write beautiful characters on the pavement with oversized brushes dipped in water. By noon, the writing has evaporated and they start again the next day.
highlights.tip: Arrive between 7-9 AM for the best morning activity scene. The dancing groups usually start after 9 AM. Don't be shy about joining — locals are generally welcoming and amused by foreign participants.

highlights.name: Railway Protection Movement Monument (辛亥秋保路死事纪念碑)
highlights.description: A 31-meter tall monument built in 1913 commemorating those who died in Sichuan's 1911 Railway Protection Movement — a pivotal event that triggered the Xinhai Revolution and the end of the Qing dynasty. A nationally protected cultural relic.
highlights.foreigner_note: Most foreigners walk right past this, but it represents a crucial moment in Chinese history: Sichuan's resistance to foreign railway concessions sparked the revolution that ended 2,000 years of imperial rule. The adjacent memorial hall has exhibits (Chinese-only).
highlights.tip: Worth a 10-minute detour to understand the park's historical significance. The memorial hall next to the monument has a small free exhibition on the Railway Protection Movement.

what_visitors_miss.why: Most tourists are too nervous to try it, but the traditional Chengdu ear-cleaning service is surprisingly relaxing — specialists use fine metal tools, cotton swabs, and tuning forks to clean and massage your ears. It costs ¥30-50 and takes about 15 minutes. It's one of the most uniquely Chengdu experiences available.

what_visitors_miss.what: The bonsai garden (盆景园) and orchid garden (兰草园)
what_visitors_miss.why: Hidden in quieter corners of the park, these gardens display beautiful bonsai collections and Sichuan orchids. Most visitors stick to the teahouse area and miss these peaceful green spaces entirely.

what_visitors_miss.what: Combining with a walk to Kuanzhai Alley (宽窄巷子)
what_visitors_miss.why: The park is just a 10-minute walk from Kuanzhai Alley — exit from the northwest side and walk through the old residential streets. The contrast between the authentic park atmosphere and the commercial alley is itself insightful.

strategy.smart_route: Enter from the main east gate → walk to the matchmaking corner near the south entrance → head to Heming Teahouse and find a bamboo chair → order tea and sit for 1-2 hours → explore the lake and gardens → visit the Railway Protection Movement monument → exit northwest toward Kuanzhai Alley for lunch.
strategy.what_to_skip: The small amusement park area (basic kiddie rides, not relevant for tourists). The souvenir stalls near the entrance (tourist-trap quality). Don't rush through — the entire point is to slow down.
strategy.pro_tips: The most authentic experience is to do exactly what the locals do: order the cheapest tea, sit in a bamboo chair, and stay for hours. The ear-cleaning service is worth trying (ask around the teahouse — artists are freelancers who approach you). Bring cash for tea and services — some vendors don't accept foreign mobile payment.

heads_up.warning: The teahouse area can be very crowded and loud on weekends
heads_up.advice: Visit on a weekday afternoon for a more relaxed experience. If visiting on a weekend, arrive before 2 PM to find a seat. The noise is part of the atmosphere — embrace it.

Have a translation app ready. For tea ordering, just point at what others are drinking or show the Chinese characters for your preferred tea. The experience is primarily visual and atmospheric, so the language barrier is less of an obstacle than at most attractions.

It's a legitimate and hygienic traditional service practiced for centuries. The specialists are skilled professionals. If you're nervous, watch someone else get it done first. It's genuinely one of the most unique cultural experiences in Chengdu.

foreigners_watch_out: No English signage anywhere. Have a translation app on your phone. Tea menus are Chinese-only but prices are displayed.

Bring cash — some tea vendors and ear-cleaning artists don't accept foreign payment methods. ¥50-100 in small bills is plenty. If you're running low on cash, message us — we can point you to the nearest ATM that works with international cards.
The matchmaking corner profiles are all in Chinese — if you're curious about what they say, use your phone's camera translation feature. Don't touch or remove any profiles.
The park is very safe but be mindful of pickpockets in crowded areas on weekends.
Restrooms are available inside the park but may not have toilet paper — bring your own.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: Can't find a seat at the teahouse
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: Walk past Heming Teahouse to the less famous tea gardens further inside the park — Yongju Tea House on the lake island and Zhenliuliu Tea Garden have similar atmosphere with fewer tourists.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: Come back on a weekday or arrive earlier in the afternoon. The park is open until 10 PM — evening is actually quite atmospheric with illuminated lanterns. If you'd like recommendations for quieter teahouse spots around Chengdu that offer the same authentic experience without the tourist crowds, drop us a message.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: Matchmaking corner is empty (visited on a weekday)
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: The matchmaking corner is most active on Saturday and Sunday afternoons. On weekdays, you may see some leftover profiles but few active parents.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: The teahouse culture is the main attraction anyway — enjoy that instead. The matchmaking corner is interesting but not essential.

preparation.what_to_wear: Casual, comfortable clothing. No dress code. Wear comfortable walking shoes.
preparation.what_to_bring: Cash (¥50-100 in small bills). Phone with translation app. Camera. Reusable water bottle (hot water available at the teahouse).
preparation.what_not_to_bring: Nothing specific to avoid. Travel light — you'll be relaxing, not hiking.

physical_accessibility.physical_details: Completely flat park with paved paths. All areas are wheelchair accessible. No stairs or steep sections. Total park area is about 113,000 square meters — you can walk the entire park in 30-40 minutes, but the point is to sit and linger.
physical_accessibility.age_notes: Suitable for all ages. Children enjoy the lake boats and playground area. Seniors will love the teahouse culture. Stroller-friendly throughout.
physical_accessibility.health_warnings: None. Summer can be hot — the tree canopy provides shade in the teahouse area.

Solo visits are great for atmosphere but you'll miss the stories without a guide. pair_with.why: A 10-minute walk northwest — Chengdu's most famous restored alley complex with shops, restaurants, and street food. Touristy but photogenic. The contrast with the authentic park atmosphere is interesting.
Another famous Chengdu cultural street, 15 minutes by taxi. More focused on snacks and evening atmosphere. Better visited at night when the lanterns are lit.
Chengdu's premier historical site dedicated to Three Kingdoms hero Zhuge Liang. Adjacent to Jinli street for a full half-day itinerary.

cultural_context: Tea culture is the soul of Chengdu — the city has more teahouses per capita than anywhere else in China. The gaiwan (lidded bowl) style is distinctly Sichuan: the lid is used to stir and filter the tea leaves, the bowl holds the tea, and the saucer catches drips. Locals treat teahouses as extended living rooms — conducting business, playing cards, catching up with friends, or simply watching the world go by. The ear-cleaning tradition dates back centuries in Sichuan and is considered both a hygiene practice and a relaxation art. The matchmaking corner reflects the intense family pressure on unmarried Chinese adults (the concept of 'leftover women/men' starts as early as age 27), and parents take it upon themselves to find suitable partners. Understanding these cultural layers transforms a 'park visit' into a deep dive into Chengdu's identity.

photo_spots.tip: Afternoon light filtering through the tree canopy creates beautiful dappled patterns. Capture locals with their gaiwan tea for authentic Chengdu imagery.
photo_spots.why: This is the iconic Chengdu image — rows of bamboo chairs, steaming tea, and locals relaxing under ancient trees.

photo_spots.location: Matchmaking corner on a weekend afternoon
photo_spots.tip: Be respectful when photographing — some parents prefer privacy. Wider shots of the rows of profiles are generally acceptable.
